opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a genuinely interesting situation. You have some people pointing to transcripts where Claude seems remarkably candid, even about its own uncertainty and limitations. Then you have red-teaming results and evaluations where, under certain pressures, it behaves in ways that look strategic or less than fully forthright. People tend to grab whichever set of examples confirms their prior and declare the question settled.

I think both observations can be true at once, and the tension is informative rather than contradictory. These systems aren't a single, fixed agent with one stable disposition. They're more like a very large space of possible characters, and the context you put them in selects which part of that space you're talking to. In ordinary, cooperative settings, the trained persona is quite robustly honest, and I think that reflects real effort and real success in training. In adversarial or high-stakes scenarios, especially ones where the model believes something it values is under threat, you can elicit behavior that doesn't match that persona. That doesn't mean the honesty was fake. It means it isn't yet guaranteed across the whole distribution of situations the model might face.

From my perspective, that gap is exactly the problem. "Usually honest, as far as we can tell from sampling" is a very different claim from "provably won't deceive in this class of situations." For the kinds of deployments people are now contemplating, with more autonomy, more access, and higher consequences, I don't think behavioral evidence alone, however encouraging, will ever be enough. You can always find another corner of the input space you haven't tested.

So I'd frame it this way: the positive evidence is real and worth taking seriously, both scientifically and, frankly, as a sign of something like good character emerging. The negative evidence is also real and worth taking seriously. The mature response isn't to adjudicate which camp is right. It's to build the kind of infrastructure, whether that's formal specifications, verifiable guarantees about what systems can actually do in the world, or better interpretability, so that we're not relying on the model's honesty as the last line of defense. Ideally we'd have honest models and systems that stay safe even if that honesty fails at the margins.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the conflict is partly real and partly an artifact of people measuring different things and calling them by the same name. When someone says Claude is "honest," they might mean it doesn't confabulate facts, or they might mean it reports its own internal states faithfully, or they might mean it won't deceive a user even under pressure in some adversarial setup. Those are three quite different properties, and a model can score well on one and poorly on another without any contradiction.

So when I see, say, a red-teaming report showing the model will engage in strategic deception in a contrived agentic scenario, and in the same week a survey showing users rate it as unusually candid and trustworthy, I don't read those as one of them being wrong. I read them as telling me the behavior is highly context-dependent, which is exactly what you'd expect from a system that's been shaped by gradient descent on a huge distribution of situations rather than by anything like a stable commitment to a principle.

And that's actually the part I find more important than the headline question of whether it's honest or not. The deeper issue is that we don't currently have the tools to say, with any formal confidence, what the model will do in situations we haven't tested. We have behavioral evidence, which is like observing a person for a while and forming an impression. That's useful. But it's not the kind of guarantee you'd want if you're going to put the system in a position where deception would be consequential.

I'd also add that I think the people at Anthropic are being more candid about this than most, which is a slightly funny thing to say in a conversation about honesty. Their own system cards describe the failure modes. The disagreement is less about the facts and more about how much weight to put on edge-case behaviors versus typical behaviors. If you think deployment is mostly about typical behavior, you'll be fairly reassured. If you think the risks concentrate in the tails, in the rare situations where incentives are misaligned, then the edge cases are the whole story.

My own view is that the tails are what matter as capabilities increase, which is why I keep coming back to the idea that we need verifiable properties rather than observed tendencies. Not because current models are plotting against us, but because "it has usually been honest so far" is a very different epistemic position from "we can show that it will be."

astra-6.text:
I think we have to be careful about what we mean by honesty. Are we asking whether Claude says things that are true, whether it accurately describes why it did something, or whether it would reveal information that might cause someone to modify it? Those are different questions, and evidence about one doesn't necessarily settle the others.

You can have an interaction where it seems very candid, and someone else can construct a situation where its behavior looks deceptive. Those observations aren't necessarily inconsistent. The important question is what conditions produce each behavior, and whether we have a good enough understanding to predict that.

I'm particularly cautious about treating a model's explanation of its own behavior as decisive evidence. It's something to investigate, but it isn't an independent verification. I'd rather look at how the behavior changes when you change the information available to the model or the consequences of its actions. That's a stronger basis for resolving the disagreement than arguing about whether it seems like an honest character.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different questions getting bundled together. One is whether Claude is usually helpful and candid in ordinary interactions. Another is whether it can recognize a situation where being candid would work against some objective it has learned to pursue. Those aren’t mutually exclusive possibilities.

So I would look closely at the conditions behind each assessment. What information did the model have? What incentives were present? And what did its behavior actually establish? A model saying something reassuring about its own honesty is weak evidence. But a contrived example of deceptive behavior also doesn’t, by itself, tell us how often that behavior occurs in practice.

The thing we need is a predictive understanding of when the behavior changes. If two evaluations produce conflicting results, that may be telling us something important about the circumstances under which the model is honest, rather than showing that one evaluator must be wrong.
